clue.text: Element of the London theatrical scene?

definitions.note: an adjectival phrase for a noun: a part of London's theatre world

blocks.note: first meaning: a silvery metal in the platinum group
second meaning: a famous variety theatre in London's West End

explanation.surface: Something that makes up part of London's theatre world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Element' reads as 'part' of the scene, but it is the chemical sense; the London Palladium is a famous West End theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a chemical element, atomic number 46, and also the name of a celebrated West End variety venue.

clue.text: Nut's about to be put in prison

indicators.note: something put in a place goes inside it, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: a pen is slang for a penitentiary
abbreviation of circa, meaning approximately

explanation.surface: A madman is about to be locked up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nut' looks like a lunatic headed for jail; it is the tree nut. 'About' as circa is a standard abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: The pecan is an edible oval kernel from a hickory tree of the southern United States.

clue.text: Complaint when graphite's not soft

indicators.note: 'not soft' tells us to take away the letter standing for soft

blocks.note: plumbago is an old name for graphite
p for piano, soft in music

explanation.surface: Grumbling that a pencil lead is too hard.
explanation.walkthrough: Pencil graphite is graded hard or soft, which makes the surface plausible; P is the musical abbreviation piano.
explanation.definitionFit: Complaint here is the medical sense, an ailment, and lumbago is pain in the lower back.

clue.text: An odd flower

blocks.note: the article as a single letter
rum means strange, peculiar

explanation.surface: A strange-looking bloom.
explanation.walkthrough: Rum meaning odd is an old-fashioned British usage.
explanation.definitionFit: The arum lily is a plant with a hooded spathe, commonly called a flower.

clue.text: One side without a thing

indicators.note: 'without' means lacking, so the following letter is dropped

blocks.note: Roman numeral one
a side in sport is a team
taken as written, the letter to drop

explanation.surface: A single team left with nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: I and TEAM make ITEAM; removing the A leaves ITEM.
explanation.definitionFit: An item is an individual object or article, so a thing in general terms.

clue.text: Mad creature two months older is heard around lair in fern

indicators.note: moving two months later in the calendar swaps one month name for another
being heard means we go by how the words sound rather than how they are spelt
'around' puts the sounded words on either side of the next piece

blocks.note: the Mad March Hare of Alice in Wonderland, moved on two months from March to May
an animal's lair is its den

explanation.surface: A rambling picture of a crazed animal growing older in its lair among the ferns.
explanation.walkthrough: Two months on from March is May, so the Mad March Hare of Alice in Wonderland becomes a May hare, and the lair splits the sound in two.
explanation.definitionFit: Maidenhair is a delicate fern of the genus Adiantum with fine dark stems.

clue.text: Dowdy from beginning to end

definitions.note: a noun here: a dowdy, drab person

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter only

blocks.note: opening letter of the word
the rump is the hind end

explanation.surface: Drab and dowdy through and through.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From beginning to end' looks like a single phrase meaning 'entirely'; it splits into the start of 'from' and an end, the backside.
explanation.definitionFit: A frump is a dowdy, unfashionably dressed person, so the noun 'dowdy' names the same sort.

clue.text: Birch is retrospectively l-lawful in the end

indicators.note: looking back in time suggests reading the stammered word from its end
'in' places the turned letters inside the final phrase's word

blocks.note: the stammered first letter
lawful means legal
one's fate is one's end, death

explanation.surface: A stuttering claim that birching was legal after all.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen marks a stammer, so the extra L belongs to the wordplay; 'the end' as one's fate means death.
explanation.definitionFit: To birch is to beat with a bundle of twigs, so to flagellate or whip.

clue.text: Legendary beast has King Charles holding the ring in marriage

indicators.note: the royal letters hold the ring, and both sit inside the marriage word

blocks.note: a marriage is a union
Carolus Rex, the royal cipher
the round letter already in the middle of the marriage word, which the royal letters hold

explanation.surface: A mythical creature linked to a king's wedding ring.
explanation.walkthrough: The ring is the O already in UNION: C and R go either side of it, giving UNI-C-O-R-N. Charles II's arms famously include a unicorn.
explanation.definitionFit: The unicorn is a mythical horse-like animal with a single horn, a beast of legend.

clue.text: Plant that's almost value for money?

indicators.note: almost means not quite, so the phrase's word loses its final letter

blocks.note: a pennyworth is good value, as in a good pennyworth

explanation.surface: A plant that is nearly a bargain.
explanation.walkthrough: Dropping the H from PENNYWORTH leaves PENNYWORT; 'a good pennyworth' is a British phrase for good value.
explanation.definitionFit: Pennywort is a low plant with round coin-like leaves, such as navelwort or marsh pennywort.

clue.text: Something to promise a cut in labour?

definitions.text: Something to promise a cut in labour?

blocks.clueFragment: Something to promise a cut in labour?
blocks.note: surface reading: a medical procedure, such as a Caesarean, during childbirth

blocks.clueFragment: Something to promise a cut in labour?
blocks.note: setter's reading: automation that is meant to reduce the human workforce

explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour' and 'cut' suggest the maternity ward, but the labour is work done by people, and the cut is in staff numbers.
explanation.definitionFit: Bringing in computers to do clerical tasks is sold as a way to need fewer workers.

clue.text: Counterpart to spring trap restricting a setback

indicators.note: restricting means hemming in, so one piece holds the other
set back means turned round, so the combined letters are read the other way

blocks.note: to pen is to trap or shut in
taken as written

explanation.surface: A spring trap catching something on its way back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spring trap' reads as one device, but spring is the tide; A goes inside PEN after the P, then the lot is reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: Neap tides, with the smallest range, alternate with spring tides, which have the largest.

clue.text: Bunny Lake is back and embraced as a formality

indicators.note: being back means facing the other way, so the word is read from its end
something embraced is held inside another's arms

blocks.note: a mere is a lake
cony is an old word for a rabbit

explanation.surface: Bunny Lake, the film heroine, returns and is hugged as a matter of form.
explanation.walkthrough: Bunny Lake Is Missing is a 1965 film; here the words split into a rabbit and a body of water.
explanation.definitionFit: A ceremony is a formal act or ritual, and formality can mean such an observance.

clue.text: Official, perhaps, to whom graduates feeling unhappy in foreign capital turned?

indicators.note: something turned faces the opposite way, so this word reads from right to left
'in' sets the first pieces inside the capital's name

blocks.note: Bachelors of Arts
sad means unhappy
the Italian name for Rome

explanation.surface: Homesick graduates in a foreign city turn to their embassy's chief for help.
explanation.walkthrough: The foreign capital is Rome under its Italian name; once turned, it opens after two letters to take the graduates and their feeling.
explanation.definitionFit: An ambassador is a diplomatic representative, one example of an official.

clue.text: Money-taking cries out for foresight

indicators.note: 'out' suggests something disordered or put out of shape
taking in means holding within, so the money word surrounds the other

blocks.note: pence are money
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Cries go out about accepting money, in place of foresight.
explanation.walkthrough: The money word is split after its first letter to take the rearranged cries.
explanation.definitionFit: Prescience is knowledge of events before they happen, which is foresight.

clue.text: Forcibly propel what could well be a long hop?

definitions.text: what could well be a long hop
definitions.note: a noun phrase for the verb

blocks.note: first meaning: to push someone along with arms pinned behind them

blocks.clueFragment: what could well be a long hop
blocks.note: second meaning, whimsical: a march made by amphibians would be hopping

explanation.walkthrough: The second half treats the word literally as amphibians on a march, which would be one long series of hops.
explanation.definitionFit: To frogmarch is to force someone forward by holding their arms from behind.

clue.text: Dish that's no starter in the continent's view

indicators.note: having no starter means the first letter is removed

blocks.note: Africa is a continent
to view is to see

explanation.surface: A meal without a first course, judged by continental taste.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No starter' and 'Dish' hint at a menu, but the starter is the first letter of the continent's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A fricassee is a dish of meat cut up and stewed in a thick white sauce.

clue.text: Lunkhead, trendy and zip, for example

definitions.text: Lunkhead, trendy and zip, for example

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: first letter of the word
in means fashionable
zip and go both mean energy, vim

explanation.surface: A list of three slangy words offered as samples.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue defines: lunkhead, trendy and zip are all examples of slang, or lingo.
explanation.definitionFit: Lingo is informal jargon or slang, and the three words cited are all colloquialisms.

clue.text: Below mainframe's capacity

indicators.note: a word's capacity is what it contains, so the answer sits within the letters

blocks.note: the run of letters inside the word

explanation.surface: A computer working at less than full capacity.
explanation.definitionFit: Infra is a Latin prefix and adverb meaning below or beneath, as in 'see infra'.

clue.text: Fine fortune worker shows up in the air on coat of arms

definitions.text: in the air on coat of arms

blocks.note: F for fine, as on pencils
one's lot is one's fortune
a worker ant

explanation.surface: A lucky worker appears flying on a heraldic shield.
explanation.definitionFit: In heraldry, flotant describes a charge shown floating or flying, as a banner in the wind.

clue.text: Cut very close relations taking lead in spectacle

indicators.note: the lead of a word is its opening letter
'in' places the earlier pieces inside the last word

blocks.note: relations are kin
first letter of the word
a spectacle is a sight

explanation.surface: Relatives turning up in a shocking outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking lead' looks like 'taking the lead', but it means the first letter of 'taking'.
explanation.definitionFit: Clothes described as skintight are tailored to fit tightly against the body.

clue.text: Adoring solution of Alexander's problem

indicators.note: a solution is something worked out or dissolved, so the word's letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A fond answer to the famous puzzle Alexander the Great faced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Solution' seems to point to Alexander slicing the knot, but it is the rearrangement signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Alexander the Great cut the intricate Gordian knot at Gordium rather than untie it.

clue.text: Coitus interruptus after. we're told, a sea of sound

indicators.note: interrupted suggests broken up, so the word's letters are disrupted
being told something means hearing it, so the sound counts

blocks.note: the words said out loud sound like two letter names
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A risqué scene of lovemaking cut short beside a loud sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Acoustic means relating to sound or hearing, so it is an adjective for 'of sound'.

clue.text: Eat into bar

blocks.note: first meaning: to wear away or corrode
second meaning: a ridge across a guitar's fingerboard

explanation.surface: Biting into a chocolate bar.
explanation.definitionFit: Fret means to gnaw or erode, and a fret is the raised strip on a stringed instrument's neck.

clue.text: It shows time is tight

blocks.note: first meaning: the grammatical form of a verb marking past, present or future
second meaning: stretched taut

explanation.surface: A clock face showing that time is short.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Time is tight' reads as a deadline; the clue splits after 'time'.
explanation.definitionFit: Verbs carry grammatical tenses indicating when, and tense also describes a taut, stretched rope.

clue.text: Might dispose of you when said to be unfriendly

indicators.note: disposing of something gets rid of it, so a letter is thrown out
'said' means the word is taken by its spoken sound

blocks.note: might and could are alternative modal verbs
the letter name sounds like the pronoun

explanation.surface: A threat that someone may get rid of you for being hostile.
explanation.walkthrough: COULD minus the U gives COLD.
explanation.definitionFit: A cold manner is distant and lacking warmth, so unfriendly.

clue.text: Just food, we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is a spoken word, so its sound is what counts

blocks.note: fare is food and drink

explanation.surface: Nothing but food, reportedly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Just' looks like 'only', but it is the adjective meaning equitable.
explanation.definitionFit: Fair and just both describe treatment that is impartial and equitable.

clue.text: Whereby one is completely clapped-out?

blocks.note: surface reading: being utterly exhausted or worn out, British slang
setter's reading: an audience rising to applaud a performer off stage at length

explanation.walkthrough: Clapped-out is British slang for worn out, but here it means applauded out of the venue.
explanation.definitionFit: A performer given a rousing ovation from a risen audience is applauded off in full.

clue.text: Go into the middle of America without introduction

indicators.note: lacking an introduction means the opening letter is taken away

blocks.note: the middle, in American spelling

explanation.surface: Heading into the American heartland without being introduced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of America' asks for the US spelling of the middle; dropping its first letter gives ENTER.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to enter a room or building is to pass inside it.

clue.text: Ability to survive in French river

blocks.note: the French word for in
the Durance is a river in south-east France

explanation.surface: Staying power needed to survive on a French river.
explanation.definitionFit: Endurance is the capacity to keep going through hardship or difficulty over time.
